title: Nouns, Gender, and the Verb Būti
summary: Every noun is masculine or feminine and usually announces which by its ending — with one group of feminines that does not; there is no article; *būti* links a subject to a predicate noun or adjective, both standing in the nominative; and the adjective agrees in gender, out of its own class of endings.

rules.heading: Gender
rules.statement: Every Lithuanian noun is **masculine** or **feminine**. There is no neuter, and no third option to fall back on. Gender is not a claim about the thing named — *stalas* ‘table’ is masculine and *knyga* ‘book’ feminine, and neither fact is about furniture or books. It matters because it is not confined to the noun: the adjective that describes it and the pronoun that replaces it must both follow it, so a noun learned without its gender is a noun that cannot yet be used in a sentence.

rules.heading: The Endings of the Nominative Singular
rules.statement: The dictionary form of a noun usually announces its gender. Masculines end in **-as, -is, -ys** or **-us**; feminines in **-a** or **-ė**. The guide is good but not perfect, and it fails in one place: a small group of very common nouns end in **-is** and are **feminine**. There is no way to tell them from masculine *-is* nouns by looking, which is why a noun is learned with its gender and its genitive — *brolis, brolio* is masculine, *moteris, moters* feminine, and the genitive is what separates them.

paradigms.caption: Nominative singular endings
paradigms.footnote: Feminine in -is: *moteris* (woman), *akis* (eye), *naktis* (night), *širdis* (heart). These must be learned individually.

sources.citation: *Dabartinės lietuvių kalbos žodynas*, Lietuvių kalbos institutas.
sources.note: Gender and genitive for the feminine -is nouns listed in the footnote.

rules.heading: Absence of the Article
rules.statement: Lithuanian has **neither a definite nor an indefinite article**. *Namas* is at once ‘a house’ and ‘the house’; nothing in the word chooses between them, and nothing needs to. Definiteness is left to the context, and made explicit only when it matters — by a demonstrative, or by where the word is placed in the sentence. The beginner's error is not omitting an article but reaching for a word to translate one with.

rules.heading: The Nominative Case
rules.statement: Lithuanian nouns decline in **seven cases**. The first is the **nominative**: the form the dictionary gives, and the form used for the **subject** — the person or thing of which something is said. Every other case will be introduced against this one, so it is worth being clear that the nominative is not a neutral or caseless shape. It is one case among seven, doing one job.

rules.heading: The Personal Pronouns
rules.statement: The personal pronouns in the nominative are given below. The third person distinguishes gender in **both** numbers, so that English *they* answers to two Lithuanian words. Because the verb ending already carries the person, the pronoun is commonly omitted; it is put in for emphasis or contrast, much as English raises the voice.

examples.target: Aš esu mokytojas, o ji yra mokytoja.
examples.gloss: I am a teacher, and she is a teacher.

paradigms.caption: Personal pronouns, nominative

rows.label: 2nd person
cells: jūs — you (more than one, or polite)

paradigms.footnote: *jie* is used of a mixed company; *jos* only where every member is feminine.

rules.heading: The Present Tense of Būti
rules.statement: **Būti**, to be, is irregular and must be learned entire. One feature of it is not peculiar to it at all: the **third person has a single form for both numbers and both genders**. *Yra* is ‘he is’, ‘she is’ and ‘they are’ alike. Every Lithuanian verb behaves so, which is worth noticing here, because it means the third-person ending never tells you how many people are meant.

paradigms.caption: būti — present tense
paradigms.footnote: Negated by prefixing *ne-*: *nesu, nesi, nesame, nesate*. The third person is irregular: **nėra**, never *neyra*.

footnotes: *Nėra* is a contraction, not a spelling variant. Writing *neyra* is an error of grammar as much as of orthography (see ¶1).

sources.citation: Ambrazas, Vytautas (ed.), *Lithuanian Grammar*. Vilnius: Baltos lankos, 1997.
sources.note: The paradigm of *būti* and the contracted negative.

rules.heading: The Predicate Noun and Adjective
rules.statement: A noun or adjective joined to the subject by *būti* forms part of what is asserted of it, and is called a **predicate noun** or **predicate adjective**. It stands in the **nominative**, exactly like the subject — there are now two nominatives in the sentence, and only the word order and the sense say which is which. This is why *būti* is not a verb that takes an object.

rules.heading: Agreement of the Adjective
rules.statement: An adjective **agrees with its noun in gender**, whether it stands before the noun as an attribute or after *būti* as a predicate. Adjectives fall into three classes by their pair of endings: **-as / -a**, **-us / -i**, and **-is / -ė**. The class is a fact about the adjective and has nothing to do with the noun: *gražus* makes its feminine *graži* whatever noun it describes, and *didelis* makes *didelė*. Agreement therefore requires two things at once — the gender of the noun and the class of the adjective.

paradigms.caption: Adjective classes
paradigms.footnote: A class III adjective in *-is* is masculine, though the same ending on a noun may be either (¶11).

footnotes: An attributive adjective normally precedes its noun, as in English.

rules.heading: Word Order
rules.statement: Because the endings show what each word is doing, word order is **freer than in English** and is used for emphasis rather than for grammar. The unemphatic order is nevertheless subject – verb – predicate, and the learner should keep to it until there is something to emphasise. Moving a word to the front foregrounds it; it does not change who is doing what.

vocabulary.notes: Masculine -is. Compare *moteris*, feminine, which looks identical in the nominative.
Feminine although it ends in -is. Compare *akis* (eye), *naktis* (night), *širdis* (heart).
Irregular throughout the present. Third-person negative *nėra*.

drills.stem: **Stalas** is masculine and **knyga** feminine. What follows from that?
drills.explanation: Gender is not a statement about furniture (¶10); it is a fact that propagates — *stalas yra naujas* but *knyga yra nauja* (¶17). A noun learned without its gender cannot yet be put into a sentence.
options: Nothing beyond the noun itself; gender is a label in the dictionary.
The adjective describing the noun and the pronoun replacing it must follow its gender.
Tables are thought of as male and books as female.
The two nouns belong to different declensions and cannot be used together.

drills.stem: Which noun's gender **cannot** be read off its nominative ending?
drills.explanation: *-is* is normally masculine, as in *brolis*, but a small group of common nouns in *-is* are feminine, and *moteris* is one (¶11). The other three follow the table exactly. This is why the dictionary cites the genitive: *brolio* against *moters* settles it.

drills.stem: Match each noun with its gender.
drills.explanation: *brolis* and *stalas* are masculine, *moteris* and *katė* feminine — so the two real labels are each used twice, and the two nouns ending in *-is* fall on opposite sides (¶10, ¶11). Option B is what the ending table alone predicts. Options C and D reach for a third and fourth gender; Lithuanian has neither, and every noun is one of two (¶10).
columnII: common — takes either agreement, according to the person meant

drills.stem: Of the nouns **namas, moteris, katė, brolis**, how many are feminine?
drills.explanation: *moteris* and *katė*. Two of the four end in *-is*, and they differ in gender (¶11) — counting by ending gives one, which is the error the question is set to catch.

drills.stem: How is **Namas yra didelis** to be translated?
drills.explanation: Lithuanian has no article, and nothing in the sentence chooses between the two English renderings (¶12). Where definiteness must be made explicit, a demonstrative does it — but it is not required, and hunting for a word to translate *the* is the beginner's mistake.
options: Neither; an article word must be supplied first.

drills.stem: In **Mokytojas yra geras**, both *mokytojas* and *geras* are nominative. Why does that not make the sentence ambiguous?
drills.explanation: *būti* links rather than governs: it takes no object, so what follows it stands in the nominative too (¶16). Here no ambiguity arises because an adjective cannot be the subject. Option B states a word-order rule the language does not have (¶18).
options: Because *geras* is an adjective and cannot be a subject.
Because the first nominative in a sentence is always the subject.
Because *būti* takes an object, and *geras* is it.

drills.explanation: The third person is *yra* for both numbers and both genders — there is no separate plural to form (¶15). *esa* is built by analogy with *esame* and does not exist. That one form serves all third persons is a feature of every Lithuanian verb, not of *būti* alone.

drills.stem: A learner writes *Knyga neyra nauja*. What is wrong?
drills.explanation: The negative of *yra* contracts to *nėra*, and *neyra* is not a variant but an error (¶15). Note the long **ė** rather than *e* + *y*: the contraction is written with the letter that carries the length (¶2). *nauja* is correct — *knyga* is feminine (¶17).
options: The third-person negative of *būti* is the contracted **nėra**.
The negative must be written apart: *ne yra*.

drills.stem: Lithuanian has two words where English has *they*. What decides between them?
drills.explanation: *jos* is used only when every member is feminine; a mixed company takes *jie* (¶14). The masculine therefore serves as the default, which is why *jie* is much the commoner of the two.
options: Whether the group is near or far.
Whether every member of the group is feminine.
Whether the group is the subject or the predicate.
Whether the speaker is being polite.

drills.explanation: The verb ending carries the person, so the pronoun is redundant and is normally dropped (¶14). It is put back in for emphasis or contrast — *aš esu mokytojas, o ji yra mokytoja* — much as English raises the voice.
options: Because the ending *-u* already identifies the person.
Because the sentence is a predicate nominative.
Because the pronoun is only used in questions.

drills.stem: Match each masculine adjective with its feminine form.
drills.explanation: Three classes are in play: *-as / -a* for *geras* and *naujas*, *-us / -i* for *gražus*, *-is / -ė* for *didelis* (¶17). The class belongs to the adjective, not to the noun it will describe, so it cannot be guessed from context. The fifth label repeats the masculine and catches anyone who expects *didelis* to be invariable.

*diena* and *knyga* are feminine and take the feminine forms of their adjectives, each from its own class (¶17). C keeps the masculine *gražus* on a feminine noun, and D the masculine *geras* on *mokytoja* — the feminine counterpart of *mokytojas*, and feminine despite naming the same profession (¶10).

drills.stem: In **Mokytoja yra gera ir graži**, how many words agree in gender with *mokytoja*?
drills.explanation: *gera* and *graži* — two predicate adjectives, from two different classes, both agreeing with the same feminine subject (¶16, ¶17). *yra* is a verb and has no gender, and *ir* is a conjunction; neither agrees with anything.

drills.stem: **Naujas yra namas.** What has moving *naujas* to the front done?
drills.explanation: The endings say what each word is doing, so order is free and carries emphasis instead of grammar (¶18). *namas* is still the subject and *naujas* still the predicate adjective; only the weight has shifted.
options: Emphasised *naujas*, without changing who is what.

drills.stem: **Graži** is the feminine of *gražus*. Is the **i** of *graži* a vowel or a mark of softening?
drills.explanation: The softening **i** of ¶6 stands between a consonant and a **back** vowel; here nothing follows it, so it is the vowel of the syllable and carries the feminine ending of a class II adjective (¶17). A learner who has just met ¶6 tends to see softening in every written *i*.
options: A vowel: it is the ending of the feminine form.
A mark of softening, and silent.
Neither; it is part of a diphthong *ži*.

drills.stem: **Tai didelė katė.** Which statements are correct?
drills.explanation: The adjective agrees with *katė* and comes from class III (¶17). *tai* is a naming word introducing the whole predicate, not a subject that *didelė* could agree with (¶16). D is right for the reason A is: change the noun's gender and the adjective follows.
options: *tai* is the subject of the sentence.
The sentence would be *Tai didelis katinas* with a masculine noun.

drills.stem: A learner writes *Moteris yra geras*, meaning ‘The woman is good.’ Which two rules has the sentence broken, if any?
drills.explanation: One error with two rules behind it. *moteris* is feminine despite its ending (¶11), and the predicate adjective must agree with it, giving *gera* (¶17). The **case** is not wrong — a predicate adjective is correctly nominative (¶16), which is what makes option D almost right.
options: None: *moteris* ends in *-is*, so *geras* is right.
Agreement, and the assumption that *-is* marks a masculine noun.
Agreement, and the case of the predicate adjective.

drills.title: Kas čia?
drills.passage:
JONAS. Labas! Kas tu esi?
RŪTA. Aš esu Rūta. Aš esu mokytoja. O tu?
JONAS. Aš esu Jonas. Aš esu mokytojas.
RŪTA. Jonai, kas čia?
JONAS. Čia mano brolis. Jis yra Tomas.
RŪTA. O kas yra ji?
JONAS. Ji yra moteris, ji nėra mergaitė. Ji yra Ona.
RŪTA. Ona yra graži!
JONAS. Taip. Ir diena yra graži. Ačiū!

questions.explanation: Jonas says *Čia mano brolis. Jis yra Tomas.* The possessive *mano* is spoken by Jonas, so the brother is his.
*Ji yra moteris, ji nėra mergaitė.* The passage denies one and asserts the other in the same breath, which is the whole point of the line.

questions.stem: Rūta says **Aš esu mokytoja** and Jonas **Aš esu mokytojas**. Why the different endings?
questions.explanation: *mokytojas* and *mokytoja* are the masculine and feminine nouns for the same profession (¶10, ¶11). The pair is a good illustration that gender is grammatical: nothing about teaching differs between the two words.
options: The noun has a masculine and a feminine form, and each speaker uses the one matching their own gender.

questions.stem: **Ji nėra mergaitė.** Identify the form *nėra* and the case of *mergaitė*.
questions.explanation: *nėra* is the contracted negative of *yra* and is one word (¶15). *būti* takes no object, so the predicate noun stays nominative even under negation (¶16) — there is no accusative anywhere in this sentence.
options: Negated third-person present of *būti*; *mergaitė* is nominative.
Negated third-person present of *būti*; *mergaitė* is accusative.
A separate negative particle; *mergaitė* is nominative.

questions.stem: **Ona yra graži** and **diena yra graži** use the same adjective form. What does that show?
questions.explanation: *Ona* and *diena* are both feminine, so *gražus* appears as *graži* twice (¶17). The form is not invariable — with *namas* it would be *gražus* — and a verb is not something an adjective can agree with (¶16).
options: That both subjects are feminine, so the class II adjective takes its feminine form in both.
That proper names have no gender.
That the adjective agrees with *yra* rather than with the subject.

sources.note: An introductions dialogue; the grammar it rests on is ¶10–¶17.

sources.citation: Ambrazas, Vytautas (ed.), *Lithuanian Grammar*. Vilnius: Baltos lankos, 1997.
sources.note: Gender, the paradigm of *būti*, and adjective agreement.

drills.translation: — Hello! Who are you? — I am Rūta. I am a teacher. And you? — I am Jonas. I am a teacher. — Jonas, who is this? — This is my brother. He is Tomas. — And who is she? — She is a woman, she is not a girl. She is Ona. — Ona is beautiful! — Yes. And the day is beautiful. Thank you!
